Gist: DéjàView is a multi-view 3D reconstruction model that replaces the deep, billion-parameter transformer stacks of VGGT, Pi3, Depth Anything 3 and similar models with a single transformer block applied recurrently K times on DINOv2 features. At 117M parameters it matches or beats those much larger feed-forward models on pointmap and camera-pose accuracy across five benchmarks. One checkpoint also lets you choose K at inference to trade compute for accuracy. For a robotics reader, the appeal is a compact, low-memory pose-and-depth front end (under 5 GiB at 24 views) whose compute can be tuned at run time. Note that this is a computer vision paper, not a robotics paper.

Question: Recent work suggests two things. Contiguous ViT layers behave like repeated applications of similar operations (RAPTOR, Jacobs et al. 2026), and DUSt3R's decoder progressively refines pointmaps across its independently parameterized layers (Starý et al. 2025). The authors ask whether depth in reconstruction transformers is mostly buying implicit iteration paid for with redundant parameters. If so, can making the iteration explicit with weight sharing match or beat parameter scaling? They also ask whether such a model can expose step count as an inference-time knob.

Method: Each view is encoded by a DINOv2 ViT-B. The model adds 4 register tokens and a camera token (with separate parameters for the reference view), plus 2D RoPE. A single looped block, consisting of VGGT-style frame attention followed by global attention with pre-norm and LayerScale, is applied K times.

- **Time conditioning:** The block is conditioned on a continuous time interval (t_k, t_{k+1}) on a uniform partition of [0,1], rather than on a step index. A zero-initialized MLP on sinusoidal embeddings produces channel-wise gates on the attention branch, the MLP branch, and the whole output state.
- **Variable K:** K is sampled per batch from Beta(2,1) scaled to [8,16], so one set of weights covers that range.
- **Supervision:** Only the final state is supervised, with no RAFT-style per-step decoding or sequence loss.
- **Outputs:** Two shallow decoders (2 blocks, width 384) produce per-pixel depth and a 6D ray map. Poses and intrinsics are recovered from the rays following DA3, with an auxiliary camera MLP head as a faster alternative.
- **Losses:** Scale-normalized depth, depth-gradient, ray, pointmap and camera terms.
- **Two-stage training:** A second stage swaps in a convolutional, confidence-weighted depth head to remove patch-grid block artifacts. Training this head end-to-end from the start was worse.
- **Dynamics:** The authors characterize the recurrence as "directional refinement." The state norm keeps growing, but cosine similarity to the final state rises to 1 and the relative update shrinks roughly fivefold. The decoder's LayerNorm absorbs the norm growth.

Robots and setup: No robots, robot platforms, onboard sensors or simulators are used, and there are no robot tasks. Inputs are unposed RGB images only. Training uses:

- 29 public datasets, sampled with temperature weighting proportional to the square root of dataset size. Examples include Aria Synthetic Environments, WildRGB-D, TRELLIS/Objaverse, CO3D, Taskonomy, ScanNet, ScanNet++, DL3DV, TartanAir, Waymo, Mid-Air, MegaDepth, Hypersim and Virtual KITTI 2.
- 2 to 18 views per scene at 504 px longest edge.
- 128 H100 GPUs: 200K iterations for stage 1 plus 40K for the depth finetune.

Evaluation covers DTU (objects), ETH3D (outdoor/indoor high-resolution), 7-Scenes and ScanNet++ (indoor), and nuScenes (driving), with a scene-level split for ScanNet++. Metrics are relative L2 and inlier ratio (relative error under 3%) after Sim(3) alignment, plus pose AUC at 3° and 30°. Baselines are run in the authors' own framework from official checkpoints: MASt3R, MASt3R-SfM, MapAnything, Pi3, VGGT, the concurrent VGGT-Ω-1B, and DA3-L and DA3-G.

Results: Averaged over the five benchmarks, DéjàView reaches 80.3% inlier ratio and 91.8 AUC@30. The next best are Pi3 (77.4 / 88.6) and VGGT-Ω (74.8 / 90.7). Efficiency at 24 views on an A100 is 117M parameters, 75.9 TFLOPs and 4.9 GiB peak memory. For comparison:

| Model | Params | TFLOPs | Peak memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| DéjàView | 117M | 75.9 | 4.9 GiB |
| Pi3 | 959M | 153.8 | 6.6 GiB |
| VGGT | 1257M | 190 | 14.7 GiB |
| DA3-L | 356M | 71.4 | 7.3 GiB |

Notable wins in AUC@3:
- ScanNet++: 79.4, versus 76.5 for Pi3 and 29.9 for VGGT-Ω.
- ETH3D: 66.0, versus 64.1 for VGGT-Ω.
- nuScenes: 43.4, versus 42.4 for VGGT-Ω.

It is not uniformly best:
- VGGT leads DTU AUC@3 by a wide margin (96.5 vs 83.2).
- VGGT-Ω leads 7-Scenes pose (21.3 vs 13.9 AUC@3) and outdoor Rel. L2 (ETH3D 0.024 vs 0.026, nuScenes 0.055 vs 0.067).
- Pi3 is marginally better on indoor pointmaps (7-Scenes Rel. L2 0.032 vs 0.035, ScanNet++ 0.014 vs 0.015).

Ablations: All ablation variants were trained for 100K iterations on the same data and averaged over the benchmarks (Rel. L2 / IR / AUC@3 / AUC@30):

| Variant | Rel. L2 | IR | AUC@3 | AUC@30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Decoupled (16 untied blocks, same compute) | 0.056 | 61.1 | 23.0 | 82.0 |
| Weight sharing alone | 0.045 | 66.4 | 30.2 | 84.8 |
| + time-conditioned residual gates | 0.042 | 67.0 | 31.5 | 85.9 |
| + state gate (full model) | 0.040 | 69.2 | 33.3 | 86.9 |

The decoupled baseline has 16× the parameters of the shared model, so the tied-weight version wins with far fewer parameters at equal compute. Variable-K training stays within about 2 to 3% of dedicated fixed-K models at K=12 and K=16. At a reduced budget, running a proper 8-step pass beats early-exiting a 16-step pass: pose AUC@3 is 0.44 versus 0.31. Attention probing shows global attention sharpening from diffuse to the correct cross-view correspondence over iterations, despite no matching supervision.

Limitations: The recurrence does not extrapolate beyond the trained K range. AUC@3 peaks near K=16 and degrades after, and all metrics collapse well past about 30 steps as a few channels grow unboundedly. So the compute knob only works within [8,16], and you cannot "think longer" for harder scenes. Variable-K training matches fixed-K rather than improving on it. Dynamic scenes are not handled.

Caveats for robotics use:
- Efficiency is reported as FLOPs and memory, not latency.
- All baselines were re-evaluated in the authors' own pipeline.
- Outputs are scale-normalized and aligned via Sim(3), not metric.

Takeaway: Read it if you need a small, memory-light, feed-forward pose and depth estimator for multi-camera or sequence inputs, or if you are interested in weight-tied and looped transformers as an alternative to parameter scaling. The ablation showing shared weights beating untied layers at equal compute is the most transferable insight. Skip it if you want robot experiments, metric-scale outputs, real-time benchmarks or dynamic-scene handling. Code and model are released.
